newsitem.title: UK: N.Irish police question four over IRA attack.
newsitem.headline: N.Irish police question four over IRA attack.

text.p: Northern Ireland police questioned four men on Tuesday over a daylight IRA rocket attack on Belfast's main court house which raised fears of retaliation by pro-British Loyalist gunmen.

Security forces were on high alert against further attacks by the Irish Republican Army after the pro-Irish guerrillas carried out their first attack of 1997 and their first strike in Belfast city centre for months.
Police said they had detained four men for questioning over Monday's attack, in which a rocket was fired at a security post outside the Courts of Justice, injuring a policeman.

The IRA, fighting to drive Britain from Northern Ireland and unite the province with the Irish republic, claimed responsibility for the attack. The guerrillas also caused city centre chaos with hoax calls claiming other devices had been left at Belfast hotels and transport centres.

British Prime Minister John Major, architect of a slow-moving Northern Ireland peace process, said the rocket attack made it hard to believe that the IRA's political wing, Sinn Fein, could take part in the peace negotiations.
Sinn Fein, led by Gerry Adams, is excluded from the talks until the IRA calls a permanent halt to a campaign of violence it launched in February last year when it ended a 17-month truce.
"It is certainly going to be extremely difficult to see how the IRA can persuade anyone that Sinn Fein should re-enter the talks," Major told BBC radio.

"It's a very odd message from Mr Adams. We believe in peace, he says, and here's another bomb or two to prove it. I don't think that is the right way to get Sinn Fein into inclusive talks and it is certainly not the right way to make progress," Major said
He was reacting to a statement by Adams which said that Britain's failure to call all-party talks without any conditions had "let the genie out of the bottle".

Police said they feared that the latest IRA attack would put further strain on a 26-month-old truce by the republican guerrillas' ideological opposites -- Protestant Loyalists who want the province to stay British.

Spokesmen for political groups close to the Loyalists said that as far as they knew the ceasefire was still intact. But weekend press reports quoted Loyalist activists as saying they would avenge IRA violence with attacks of their own.
